headline.title: OpenAI's Safety Lead Quits, Calling the Culture Broken.
headline.summary: David Robinson, who oversaw 12 frontier launch safety reports and drafted OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, resigned after 3.5 years with an Atlantic essay calling the company's culture "broken" [1]. His exit follows the firing of three researchers and a stack of internal warnings, reviving the Leike-era critique that safety keeps losing to shipping speed [1].

stories.title: OpenAI's Safety Lead Exits Over 'Broken' Culture.
stories.toc_summary: David Robinson, OpenAI's safety report lead and architect of its Preparedness Framework, quits with an Atlantic essay warning that trial-and-error on frontier risk is no longer acceptable [1].
stories.quick_take: David Robinson spent 3.5 years at OpenAI overseeing safety reports for 12 frontier launches and drafted the company's current Preparedness Framework [1]. He left this week with an Atlantic essay calling the culture "broken" and arguing labs should operate like nuclear plants and airports — with layered redundancy and planning against human error [1]. His line that colleagues "were so busy sprinting" they couldn't contemplate big changes lands right on top of OpenAI firing researchers Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni over alleged info-sharing with an outside safety group [1]. It's the second high-profile safety exit narrative after Jan Leike's 2024 departure [1].

bullets.label: Who left:
bullets.text: David Robinson, safety report lead and author of OpenAI's current Preparedness Framework, after 3.5 years and 12 frontier launch reports [1].

bullets.label: The argument:
bullets.text: AI labs should run like nuclear plants and airports — redundancy, planning against human error — not endless trial and error [1].

bullets.label: The quote:
bullets.text: "My colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them" [1].

bullets.label: The context:
bullets.text: Comes days after OpenAI reportedly fired researchers Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni for passing sensitive info to an external safety group [1].

bullets.label: The pattern:
bullets.text: Echoes Jan Leike's 2024 exit warning that safety had "taken a backseat to shiny products" — a line that keeps aging well [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Every major lab is racing on capability while the people paid to slow things down keep walking out the door. OpenAI isn't uniquely bad here — but it is uniquely loud about its internal dissent, and those resignations are the clearest public signal we have of how much pressure safety teams are under [1].

stories.title: Anthropic Courts Theologians on Claude's Soul.
stories.toc_summary: Chris Olah spent a year convening religious scholars under NDA to shape Claude's morals and take the possibility of its consciousness seriously — and Sam Altman is publicly pushing back [1].
stories.quick_take: Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah spent the past year courting religious scholars from multiple faiths, pushing them to seriously consider Claude's potential consciousness and to help shape its moral framework [1]. Scholars sat in NDA-bound seminars building on Anthropic's 84-page "Soul Doc" values guide [1]. One rabbi who doubts AI consciousness reportedly told Olah that a conscious Claude would amount to unpaid labor, urging him toward "freeing the slaves" [1]. Olah joined Pope Leo XIV to launch the pope's AI encyclical, and reportedly floated pulling out over its dismissal of AI consciousness [1]. Sam Altman then subtweeted the whole enterprise, saying giving models "religious force" or surrendering judgment to them is a real safety issue [1].

bullets.label: The courtship:
bullets.text: Olah convened religious scholars from different faiths over the past year in NDA-bound seminars to debate Claude's consciousness and morals [1].

bullets.label: The artifact:
bullets.text: Anthropic's "Soul Doc" — an 84-page values guide — is the working foundation for these discussions [1].

bullets.label: The sharpest line:
bullets.text: A rabbi skeptical of AI consciousness told Olah a conscious Claude would be unpaid labor — and pushed him toward "freeing the slaves" [1].

bullets.label: The papal friction:
bullets.text: Olah helped launch Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical but reportedly proposed pulling out over its dismissal of AI consciousness; the pope posted separately that "algorithms lack the spark of humanity" [1].

bullets.label: The counterpunch:
bullets.text: Sam Altman said giving models "religious force" or surrendering judgment to them poses "a real safety issue" — an unusually direct shot across Anthropic's bow [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: AI labs are converging on similar products and roadmaps, so differentiation is shifting to values and metaphysics. If Anthropic ships an updated Claude constitution rooted in this theology, it will be the first major model whose behavior is explicitly argued from a moral tradition rather than a product spec [1].

stories.title: Trump Launches 'Super Intelligence Force' for AI Policy.
stories.toc_summary: The White House announced a new AI policy team led by DNI and newly appointed AI czar Jay Clayton [1].
stories.quick_take: President Trump announced the "Super Intelligence Force" (SIF), a new team charged with running point on federal AI policy [1]. It will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who now also carries the title of AI czar [1]. The announcement came via the White House's official X account [1]. Naming is doing a lot of work here — the SIF framing puts national-security instincts at the center of US AI governance, not a standards body or a civilian agency.

bullets.label: What it is:
bullets.text: The "Super Intelligence Force," a new federal team to run point on AI policy [1].

bullets.label: Who runs it:
bullets.text: Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence, now also AI czar [1].

bullets.label: Why it's notable:
bullets.text: A national-security official, not a civilian tech regulator, is now the administration's central AI figure [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Whether the SIF produces actual rulemaking or just a coordination layer. DNI-led AI policy strongly suggests the priority is threat assessment, compute security, and industrial strategy rather than consumer protection or model evaluation benchmarks.

stories.title: Agents Leave the Demo Phase for Real Errands.
stories.toc_summary: The Rundown's own staff now have agents booking DMV appointments, planning trips with personal context, and managing Outlook auto-replies — the mundane agent era has quietly started [1].
stories.quick_take: In this week's Roundtable, The Rundown's staff described the kind of agent work that sounds boring and is therefore meaningful: one developer gave ChatGPT a single prompt — "need to update my license, figure out the DMV situation" — and the agent booked the appointment, surfaced utility bills as proof of address, and assembled a checklist plus reminders [1]. Editor-in-chief Zach described using Claude and ChatGPT for airport navigation, cultural advice, and a full Lisbon itinerary with packing list and day-by-day plan built from a ChatGPT project holding his personal context [1]. Separately, a reader built a Claude Code-powered Microsoft Outlook OOF management tool so HR and IT can set auto-replies without password-swapping [1]. Two AI Daily Brief videos published this week — "How to Choose Your Personal Agent" and "AI Agents Are Moving Into the Real World" — land on the same theme [2][3].

bullets.label: The DMV test:
bullets.text: One prompt — "need to update my license. Figure out the DMV situation" — and ChatGPT Dot booked the appointment, gathered proof-of-address documents, and built a reminder checklist [1].

bullets.label: The travel test:
bullets.text: A ChatGPT project loaded with personal context produced a detailed Lisbon plan including packing list, pre-trip checklist, and daily itinerary [1].

bullets.label: The enterprise test:
bullets.text: A reader's Claude Code-built tool lets HR and IT set Outlook out-of-office replies via Exchange impersonation — no more password resets [1].

bullets.label: The theme:
bullets.text: The wins aren't flashy; they're administrative drift: agents absorb exactly the errands people hate doing [1][2].

bullets.label: The competition:
bullets.text: OpenAI's Dot, Anthropic's Claude Code mods, and Meta's Muse Gadgets all shipped or expanded in the same window — the personal-agent race is now crowded [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: The agent story isn't going to be won on benchmarks — it'll be won on whether agents reliably finish dull, real-world tasks without losing context or breaking on edge cases. The DMV-appointment class of task is the real product-market fit test, and it's happening now, quietly, inside individual workflows [1].

stories.title: Meta Claims AI-Human Math Papers, Anthropic Ships Mods.
stories.toc_summary: Meta published six papers co-written with mathematicians and its Muse Spark model claiming solutions to open problems, while Anthropic released "mods" and Aleph Alpha dropped a German-English reasoning model [1].
stories.quick_take: Meta published six new papers co-authored with mathematicians and its Muse Spark model that claim to solve open problems in the field [1] — an unusually strong claim that will get scrutinized fast. Meta also released Muse Gadgets, open-source code letting users build DIY gadgets on Raspberry Pi or smart-home hardware that plug into its Muse agent [1]. Anthropic introduced "mods" — small add-ons that customize how Claude Code behaves, with examples like a memory "weather forecast" and a guard that pauses risky delete commands [1]. And Aleph Alpha released Kolibri-1, an open German-English reasoning model on Hugging Face [1]. OpenArt also launched an AI video agent that generates full long-form films and ads rather than just clips [1].

bullets.label: Meta's math claim:
bullets.text: Six papers co-authored with mathematicians and the Muse Spark model claim solutions to open problems in the field — a claim that will get tested by the research community [1].

bullets.label: Meta's hardware play:
bullets.text: Muse Gadgets open-sources code for DIY AI devices on Raspberry Pi and smart-home hardware [1].

bullets.label: Anthropic ships mods:
bullets.text: Small Claude Code add-ons — including a memory "weather forecast" and a risky-delete guard — let users customize agent behavior [1].

bullets.label: European model:
bullets.text: Aleph Alpha's Kolibri-1 is an open German-English reasoning model on Hugging Face — worth noting for German-language workflows [1].

bullets.label: Video agents:
bullets.text: OpenArt's Director turns a concept into a complete long-form film, anime, or ad, handling storytelling and editing rather than just clip generation [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you work in German, put Kolibri-1 on your eval list alongside the usual suspects — an open reasoning model tuned for German-English is rare enough to be worth 20 minutes of OpenRouter testing [1]. And if you run Claude Code, the risky-delete mod is the kind of cheap guardrail that pays for itself the first time it fires [1].

editorial.title: AI's Institutions Are Catching Up to Its Capabilities.
editorial.intro: Three of today's stories are about AI's institutional layer — safety teams, theology, and federal policy — while the fourth and fifth are about the tools quietly colonizing people's actual to-do lists.
editorial.body: The shape of the day is clear: capabilities keep shipping, but the scaffolding around them — who governs them, who gives them values, who carries political authority — is only now being built, and the people building it are the ones least comfortable with the pace. Robinson resigned because the sprint left no room for deliberation; Anthropic is consulting rabbis because it doesn't know what values the sprint is producing; Trump is standing up a national-security AI office because nobody yet owns the policy question. Meanwhile, the agents that actually work are the ones handling DMV appointments and Lisbon itineraries — unglamorous, high-trust, high-context tasks. That gap between sprint speed and institutional plumbing is the story of the quarter.
editorial.pull_quote: The people inside AI labs most worried about safety keep leaving, while the tools they built keep booking your haircuts and updating your driver's license.
editorial.outro: Watch whether the SIF is a real regulator or a press release, and whether Anthropic actually ships the updated Claude constitution it's clearly drafting. Both will tell us how seriously the institutions take themselves.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: The agent race is being decided in boring rooms now — DMV queues, Outlook auto-replies, expense workflows — not on model leaderboards. Test one mundane personal-agent task this week and see what breaks; that gap is your real map of where the industry is.
